claims.text: A hybrid framework can separately compute electron–phonon-mediated electronic transport and anharmonic phonon transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit treatment of oxygen defects will enable prediction of transport in oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr.
The hybrid framework will improve overall predictive accuracy by roughly 30–50% relative to Debye-based and DFT-elasticity methods.
The proposed model covers ideal defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions of HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Experimental total-conductivity data for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr span 300–1200 K.
Incorporating oxygen defects into interatomic potentials will adjust scattering rates and phonon lifetimes.
Separately calculating electronic and phononic scattering and conductivity prevents conflation of the two thermal-transport channels.
Detailed treatment of channel-specific scattering under realistic defect conditions will improve the accuracy of conductivity predictions as functions of temperature and oxygen level.
At 300 K, the predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be approximately 6–10 W/(K·m).
At 300 K, the predicted electronic thermal conductivity will be approximately 4–7 W/(K·m).
The summed 300 K conductivity will fall within the reported experimental range of 10–17 W/(K·m) for oxygen-doped HfNbTaTiZr.
Separate low-temperature predictions will reproduce comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K.
Earlier Debye-temperature and DFT-elasticity approaches conflated lattice and electronic contributions.
Earlier approaches have predictive accuracy substantially lower than that of the proposed method.
The model is applicable only below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K, and only up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Approximations in ab initio and machine-learning methods make the numerical improvement and defect-scattering sensitivity uncertain.
Experimental comparison is necessary to assess the validity of transport predictions.
A discrepancy greater than ±20% in either separated conductivity, or an improvement below approximately 30%, will falsify the proposed model.
